# How to Explain What You Do as a Consultant, Author, Speaker

When someone asks you what you do at a dinner or summit, how do you respond? If you find yourself rattling off three distinct careers, you probably notice their eyes glaze over. It is easy to feel scattered when your daily reality spans advisory meetings, book manuscripts, and stage keynotes.

Trying to explain what I do consultant author speaker does not require you to compress your entire life into a tiny soundbite. Instead, it demands a clear, unified architecture that ties your intellectual property together. Once you frame your work around outcomes rather than activities, people instantly recognize your real value.

You can turn a complex, multi-hyphenate career into your greatest strategic advantage. This guide breaks down how to clarify your positioning, streamline your audience-centric messaging, and present your diverse expertise with authority.

changes.location: ## The Challenge of Explaining a Multi-Hyphenate Career
changes.before:
## The Challenge of Explaining a Multi-Hyphenate Career

When people ask what you do at a conference or networking dinner, rattling off three distinct job titles often creates cognitive dissonance for your listener. When your audience feels confused about how your roles connect, they struggle to understand how you can solve their specific business problems. A scattered list of tasks forces someone else to do the heavy mental lifting of figuring out where you fit.

Your goal is not to list every hat you wear, but to present an overarching strategic narrative that ties your consulting, writing, and speaking into one clear ecosystem. Shifting your mindset from describing your tasks to communicating your transformative impact instantly changes how prospective clients perceive you. They begin to see you as a strategic solution rather than a disconnected freelancer.

When you frame your multi-faceted work under a unified umbrella, you establish immediate credibility. You position yourself as an authority who possesses deep strategic insights, shares them broadly on stages and pages, and executes them directly for clients. That synthesis turns potential confusion into unmatched executive weight.

## How Consulting, Writing, and Speaking Reinforce One Another

Combining consulting, writing, and keynote speaking is one of the most effective business model scalability options for modern experts. Each discipline strengthens the others, creating a virtuous cycle of visibility, authority, and deep client impact. The work you do with clients fuels the stories you tell on stage and in print.

Writing a book codifies your thought leadership and gives your frameworks tangible weight, while keynote speaking broadcasts those ideas to wide executive audiences. When audience members want hands-on service implementation of your ideas, your high-touch advisory services provide the natural next step using a one-liner framework. The cycle feeds itself continuously over time.

This balanced ecosystem protects your schedule and improves business model scalability. Instead of trading hours for dollars exclusively, you use multiple touchpoints that build long-term enterprise value and client trust. Each channel deepens your authority while expanding your commercial reach through clear proof points.

changes.location: ## Unifying Your Roles into a Single Strategic Narrative
changes.before:
## Unifying Your Roles into a Single Strategic Narrative

A compelling strategic narrative weaves your various roles into a cohesive story centered on a single core mission. Instead of introducing yourself in fragments, lead with the primary business transformation you engineer for your market. Your audience needs to understand the big picture before they care about the delivery format.

Define your central thesis by identifying the common problem you solve across every channel. Whether advising a boardroom, publishing an article, or delivering a keynote address, your foundational message remains constant while only the delivery format changes. The core idea stays steady even as your medium shifts.

Focus on your ideal client persona when crafting this first person bio. When listeners hear you describe their exact pain points and business aspirations, they care less about your job titles and more about the outcomes you deliver. Relevance always builds more trust than a laundry list of credentials.

### Crafting Your person bio Value Proposition

Your personal mission statement should succinctly answer who you serve, the strategic hurdle you help them overcome, and the measurable result you create. Grounding your identity in this statement prevents you from feeling scattered when introducing your diverse offerings. It anchors every conversation in genuine business outcomes.

Keep this statement free of industry buzzwords and corporate jargon. Direct, confident phrasing signals that you possess genuine command over your subject matter and respect your client's time. Clear language shows true authority far better than inflated vocabulary.

### Using a One-Liner Framework for Instant Clarity

A proven one-liner framework helps you explain your complex career in under fifteen seconds. Start with the market problem, introduce your unique mechanism or framework, and conclude with the ultimate business benefit. This approach makes your professional bio easy to grasp immediately.

For example, rather than saying you are a leadership consultant, published author, and speaker, you might say: I help enterprise executives navigate high-stakes reorganizations through proprietary advisory frameworks, keynote presentations, and published research. This structure anchors your thought leadership in a clear, single outcome. It tells people exactly how your work changes organizations.

## Client Acquisition and Ethical Boundaries in Self-Promotion

Mastering client acquisition as an author and speaker requires knowing when and how to introduce your advisory services. Delivering exceptional value on stage or through your book builds goodwill; aggressive pitching from the stage can instantly erode that trust. True experts never need to push hard to attract serious interest.

Establish clear ethical boundaries by separating educational delivery from commercial proposals. Let your stage presence demonstrate your mastery naturally, allowing attendees to seek out your consulting engagement opportunities independently. When your insights are undeniably sharp, your audience naturally inquires about working with you directly.

Provide clear pathways for interested leaders to take the next step, such as downloading a strategic whitepaper or taking an assessment. This polite, permission-based approach naturally attracts aligned corporate partners who value your expertise. It protects your brand integrity while building a reliable client pipeline.

## Complete article manuscript

# How to Explain What You Do

For consultants, authors, and speakers.

**How do you explain what you do when you are a consultant, author, and speaker?**

Start with who you help and the specific result you help them achieve. Then explain how your consulting, writing, and speaking support that work. Use one clear sentence for the value of your expertise and a second for how people can work with you. Add a relevant example or credential when the conversation calls for it.

You have built a business, advised clients, written a book, or earned your place on a stage. Yet a simple question can still leave you giving a surprisingly complicated answer: What do you do?

The difficulty may be deciding what belongs first. Every title represents work you have earned, so leaving one out can feel like making yourself smaller.

You do not have to explain your entire career in the opening sentence. Give the other person enough context to understand your work, then let the conversation become more specific.

For an established woman with several ways of serving her audience, the useful question is: What should someone understand about my expertise before I tell them how I deliver it?

changes.location: ## Find the work your roles have in common
changes.after:
## Find the work your roles have in common

Write down the problems you address in your consulting, the ideas you teach in your book, and the subjects you speak about. Look for a specific connection you can explain without using words such as impact, empowerment, or transformation on their own.

A leadership consultant might help newly promoted managers lead former peers. Her book could teach the conversations that transition requires, while her keynote helps organizations recognize where new managers need support. Those are three ways to address a recognizable problem.

Start with that problem. Consultant describes a working relationship. Author describes published work. Speaker describes a delivery format. None of those titles, by itself, explains your subject or whom you serve.

**Three questions to find your central message**
1. Who comes to you for help, and what is happening in their life or business?
2. What can you help them understand, decide, or do?
3. Which part of that work appears across your consulting, writing, and speaking?

If there is no meaningful overlap, be honest about it. A business advisory practice and a novel may belong to different audiences. You can introduce the work relevant to the conversation without forcing every interest into a single commercial promise.

changes.location: ## Build an introduction in two sentences
changes.after:
## Build an introduction in two sentences

Use the first sentence to explain your value. Use the second to explain the ways you deliver it. This gives you a clear starting point and room to adapt.

> I help [specific people] [achieve a clear result] through [a concrete approach].

Then add: I do that through consulting, my book, and speaking. You can name the relevant format first or leave the others for a follow-up question. The wording should sound natural in your mouth.

### Illustrative introduction: a leadership expert

I help first-time managers handle difficult conversations and lead their teams with clear expectations. I teach that work through consulting, my book, and leadership workshops.

### Illustrative introduction: an experienced business owner

I help owners put the day-to-day structure in place to run a business that can operate without their constant involvement. I work with them privately and teach those principles through my writing and speaking.

These are invented examples for adaptation, not client quotes. Replace the audience, result, and approach with work you can actually support. A named method is useful when you have one; calling your advice proprietary does not make the explanation clearer.

For a casual conversation, you may only need the first sentence. For a prospective client, add what the work involves. If a familiar concern matters, address it plainly: We start with your current team and processes. Avoid attaching a promise you cannot control just to make the introduction sound stronger.

## Adapt the message to the person in front of you

Keep your central expertise consistent while changing the detail. A prospective client needs to understand how you would help. An event organizer needs to understand the audience and the session. A reader needs a reason to open the book.

### When a prospective consulting client asks

I help newly promoted managers handle the conversations they have been avoiding. In a consulting engagement, we work through real situations, clarify expectations, and practice how they will respond.

### When an event organizer asks

I speak to new managers about leading former peers. The session gives them language to set expectations, address tension, and give useful feedback.

### When a reader asks about the book

My book is for people who have become the manager of a team they used to belong to. It walks through the conversations that change when you become responsible for leading others.

All three examples describe the same area of expertise. Each answers the immediate question without requiring the listener to understand the whole business. Use this approach on your website too: a shared introduction, followed by clear pages for consulting, speaking, and books.

Do not imply that buying a book leads automatically to a consulting engagement, or that speaking will reliably generate clients. Give interested people an appropriate next step, such as exploring your consulting page or sending a speaking inquiry.

changes.location: ## Turn the introduction into a useful professional bio
changes.after:
## Turn the introduction into a useful professional bio

A professional bio needs more context than a spoken introduction, but the same order works: expertise, audience, relevant proof, and ways to engage. Choose the details that help this particular reader judge your fit.

Use first person for a conversational introduction or personal About section when that suits your voice. Use third person when an organizer needs copy to introduce you. Follow the requested format and length rather than trying to force one bio into every setting.

### First-person bio template

I help [audience] [specific outcome] through [approach]. My work draws on [relevant, verified experience]. Through [consulting offer], [book title], and [speaking topic], I help people [concrete application]. Learn more about [appropriate next step].

### Third-person speaker bio template

[Name] is a [relevant specialty] consultant, author, and speaker who helps [audience] [specific outcome]. Drawing on [verified experience or credential], she teaches [specific subject]. Her session helps attendees [realistic takeaway].

These are working templates. Remove any placeholder you cannot fill truthfully. If the book is still in progress, say that. If you have not delivered paid keynotes, do not imply that you have. Your actual experience deserves a clear explanation.

### Keep the headline clear at a glance

For a LinkedIn profile or website heading, lead with your specialty and audience. For example: Leadership consultant for first-time managers | Author | Speaker. Use the surrounding copy to explain the result and provide evidence. Avoid packing the headline with every credential and every topic you have ever taught.

A personal detail can make a longer bio feel more like you, but it should not displace the information someone needs to understand your work. Your hobbies are optional. Your area of expertise is not.

Choose evidence that supports the work you want to be hired for. A recording can show how you teach on stage. A published book demonstrates the ideas you have developed. A documented client example can show the kind of problem you have helped address.

Be precise about your contribution and the outcome. A speaking inquiry is different from a booked engagement. An engagement is different from a completed paid keynote. Share client details only when you have permission, and give the context needed to understand a result.

### How an established business can support a wider personal brand

FORDIVINE’s [Michelle Roby case study](https://www.fordivine.com/crowned-stories/michelle-roby) describes how her experience as a business owner became the basis for consulting and speaking. The relevance here is the connection between her existing experience and the work she wanted to offer. It is a documented client example, not a promise that changing a bio produces the same result.

For your own introduction, keep one example ready. When someone asks how your approach works, explain a relevant situation, what you did, and what changed. You do not need to recite your entire resume to make the next sentence credible.

## Test whether people can explain your work back to you

Say your introduction aloud to someone who does not already know your business. Ask them whom they would refer to you and what they think you would help that person do. Their answer is more useful than a polite compliment.

**Check the explanation before you publish it**
1. Can someone identify your audience without asking three more questions?
2. Does the result mean something concrete to that audience?
3. Can you support the expertise and experience you claim?
4. Do your website, bio, and speaking page describe compatible work?
5. Is the next step clear for someone who wants to hire you?

If the explanation keeps expanding, return to the decision beneath the copy. You may still be choosing which audience to prioritize or which part of your work you want to grow. More polished wording cannot make that decision for you.

If the uncertainty extends across your offers and public presence, explore [how a complete brand engagement works](https://www.fordivine.com/discover). The introduction should reflect decisions your wider brand can carry through.

## Questions about introducing a multifaceted career

### Should I call myself a consultant, author, or speaker first?

Lead with the role most relevant to the setting, or start with the problem you help solve. In a speaking inquiry, your speaking topic belongs early. In a consulting conversation, explain your specialty and the client need. You can include the other roles once the central value is clear.

### Can I keep consulting, writing, and speaking under one personal brand?

Yes, when they share a credible connection in expertise, audience, or purpose. Explain that connection, then give each offer a clear place. If the audiences and subjects are unrelated, use distinct descriptions or sections so visitors can find the work relevant to them.

### How long should my answer to “What do you do?” be?

Start with one or two sentences and leave room for a response. Add detail when the person asks or when the setting requires it. The test is whether they understand your work, not whether you have reached a particular word count.

### What if I serve more than one audience?

Name the audience relevant to the conversation and be explicit about the problem you address for them. On your website, explain the shared expertise first, then help each audience find its own offer. Avoid a broad promise that obscures meaningful differences in your work.
